review_text_raw:
A very introspective look at UNIX commands and the general actions of hacking - which is basically accurate, but taking out the time required to accomplish these things (for example, you can solve port protocols within a few seconds, but IRL this might take hours).

Basically, if you want the "reality" where you are the hacker in one of these movies (you're not playing the hacker, but ARE the hacker), then this is pretty spot-on. It just removes most of the tedium of the acitivites. This is not to say that the game isn't repetitive; it is, and remains true to its roots as a simulator. By nature, most simulators run off of repetitive actions which require muscle memory and timing in order to complete.

In actual fact, this is more of a puzzle-solving game. However, combined with some funny easter eggs (IRC chats can get hilarious) and honest-to-god methodology on the principles of hacking, this actually becomes enjoyable unless you just want to shoot things in the face (in which case, this is NOT the game for you).

Anyone who wants to work in software QA should be able to play this game comfortably, figure out most of the puzzles, and genuinely enjoy the experience. If you can't, don't take QA as a career. Because this in almost any form is what you do - all day, every day. I know this from 14 years of experience at that job in everything from game development to SAS or security software.

There are a few points I wish there were more of, or more developed. As game, it's pretty linear. There are nice little things like finding additional information on a server which gives you another terminal to hack, or a phone to break into, but these are too few and far between. It could be far more sandboxy if there were a freeform mode for points, which had sets of systems and connected devices which would allow you to randonly investigate things you found on another system. In this, you'd need a points system or something to gain (money, cred, whatever) - which would be a welcome addition to the game. I think another fun mode would be to actually use the system specs for the computer it was running on for memory, etc. as well as randonly generating in-game groups to become involved with, do missions for (from forums, etc.)

I recommend this game, just due to the simulation nature being captured very well. That being said, this game won't be for everyone. Much of the game is tedium and random investigation - which is exactly what hacking is about. One of the best missions which represents this is the "Project Junebug" mission. You're basically let loose to figure out how to accomlish the task, you have a lot of reading to do to catch up on how to accomplish it, and there isn't any handholding. YOU have to do the tasks, to the best of your understanding, and figure out indeed, what those tasks are, and it involves multiple servers, and different methods of having the same outcome.

Pros:

1. It's simple and pretty straight forward
2. You never (mostly) are left in the dark about what to do next
3. You can be a "real" Hacker for once
4. Simple and understandable UI
5. Learn some Linux commands
6. Great Storyline
7. The atmosphere and tense you get while hacking
8. A lot of hidden ingame stuff
9. The DLC "Labyrinths"

Neutral:

1. I can imagine that the music is not for everyone
2. Way too simple and straight forward compared to Uplink
3. Limited Options (while in Uplink you can hack Banks to get money or even give it to someone else, destory/save lives by manipulating police entries and such)
4. Missing does insane minigames, from Uplink, to crack a Lan and the option to build your own computersetup 

In-Depth Review:

I don't know if people still know that gem of a game called "Uplink". It's from the Year 2001 and was one of the best science fiction games back then (still is, but didnt aged very well). Hacknet is just a modern version of "Uplink". But it's extremly simplified compared to it, which have it's pros and it's cons of being so ofc. While Hacknet never reaches that incredible Depth Uplink offered, it's still have a lot of great moments itself, mostly because of a good storyline you can follow.

Hacknet is basically a pure text-based game in a science fiction setting. You are hacking computers, databases and other stuff 100% of the time. You wont do anything else. Don't except to buy your own computerparts, or anything like that. Playtime is around 10-20 hours and more if you have the DLC. 

The game is pretty easy and very straight forward. I have the feeling the game is holding your hands for a bit too long. But when it finally let you loose, oh boy, the felling of power and control is just awesome. There so many secrets to discover and little hidden stuff to look out for, it keeps you occupied for a few hours. And the music (it varies, but sometimes it's psytrance-like music and you get the felling you are on a Goa-Party) is pushing you all the time. You really fell like a "Supa Hacka" at times.

If you like the basegame, check out the DLC "Labyrinths" as well, because it lets you loose right from the start. It offers a own storyline to follow, new features, executables and Themes. 

Overall Hacknet and it's DLC, surely is worth the money if you like text-based adventures, want to learn/relearn a few basic Linux/Dos commands on the way, looking for a new Uplink for years (like myself), or just want to be a "Supa Hacka" for once.

This was incredibly thrilling to play. The push for speed challenged your ability to retain information in a short period of time, and it was an incredible experience. It's not real coding, like others have mentioned, so you're not going to learn anything. You essentially learn how to use prebuilt tools in a command prompt and how to communicate with a computer. But it works like a virtual machine with its own language and a fake operating system. (And I think that's really cool). It's also pretty cool that you can see your actual computer's command prompt when you minimize the game, essentially seeing how this virtual machine is talking to your computer.

However, there are gripes.

The ability to lock yourself out of beating the game without knowing it is really easy. You have to be VERY mindful of your actions. Deleting the wrong thing can trap you and force you to start a new game entirely.  

There are also some bugs, mostly involving how the quest system operates. That can also get stuck, especially if you already have a grasp of what you need to do, you can outrun your quest and cause it to lock up. Pace yourself.

Lastly, having content that is procedurally generated is awesome, but I felt like the game struggled between being "open world" and linear. If you want a game where you can investigate to find the story, open world is a wonderful option, but a linear story is great too if you're immersive enough.

Overall, if you want an experience that's an "idea" of hacking, you should definitely try this game.

If the developers make another game like this, I'd be interested in playing that one too. Maybe a sequel? I love the concept, but I'd really hope for a more open world experience.

Hacknet is an excellent hacking simulator. Its user interface is very convincing and sleek, and there is just enough recognizable computer-jargon to make it somewhat realistic without making it boring or too dense to understand. Using the command terminal is way faster (and way cooler) then just using the GUI and makes you feel like you're the real deal.

Downsides to the game are the occasional spelling mistakes and the lack of explanation at some points in the game. My biggest issue with the game, however, is the complete linearity of the game. It never feels like you're interacting with a bigger world around you, just a pre-determined set of servers you have to hack, which is a shame. If it could be expanded somewhat to include a more dynamic 'internet' for you to explore, and more leeway in how to approach missions, this would've been the new standard in hacking sims. As is, it's a great game, but Uplink still holds the title.

Before coming across Hacknet I first played Uplink. A hacking game quite like this one. I thoroughly enjoyed it, and when I came across Hacknet on the store page when it was released I loved the idea of a newer version. Little did I know I was stumbling across potentially one of the best games I have ever played!

Unlike other games, Hacknet's beautiful story is woven into dialogue and .txt files. Some of these are hidden so you feel like the story is being slowly unveiled to you until you finally discover what is happening.

The gameplay is one of the things I quite enjoy about this game. You begin with simple tools allowing you to access lightly secured systems. As the game progresses, you gain more tools and skills until you are hacking your way into complex and difficult systems. This feels quite satisfying to grow from a beginner into a skilled hacker. As you explore the systems in Hacknet, you are encouraged to dig deeply into the systems, often uncovering interesting parts of the story and some rather comical dialogue. The game also puts you on edge, as when you begin you are told you are being tracked and are encouraged to always remember to cover your tracks. This feeling becomes quite exhilarating as you are hacking into secure systems and deleting your tracks with seconds to spare for your own safety.

Overall, this game is unlike Uplink, the game I expected it to be like. And is an amazing gem of a game in it's own way. If you're looking for a game that gives you the experience of hacking, being constantly under threat with great gameplay and a beautiful story. I highly recommend this game.

Most of the gameplay is done through the terminal, you'll use the classic UNIX commands to navigate the devices you hack giving it quite a realistic feel. Of course this is still a game, so you don't have to look at the MAN pages to understand how to hack. At it's core it's a detective game, and the crime scene is the network which you explore little by little. One critique I have is that every exploit doesn't feel different enough, sure, you get different graphics but I think some kind of minigame would have made each exploit script a bit more interesting. The story was quite interesting and the game provides some comedic relief in the form of IRC chat logs that are quite enjoyable. If you're fun of secrets in games you'll find quite a few here. All in all, solid indie game, very unique experience that, if you aren't scared of reading a little, will be fun and rewarding.

This game was a little difficult to start, and there were some parts that did not seem very intuitive as far as username hacking is concerned.  But overall, I really liked this game.  Has an original MS DOS feel to it with the HackNet interface that really got me into it.  Seemed quite immersive in that way.  The story is good also.  It was sad when I first noticed the "0".  

Pros: Good story.  Great interactivity.  100% dependence on player to advance story.  There are no question marks over the node you have to access next.  You have to discover where you have to go to get the information you need.  

Cons: Story can get a little disconnected at times.  All information provided does not always seem to point clearly to the answer needed to progress the next step (but this might just be my mind not putting A and B together correctly).

Would totally recommend if you are interested in trying an indie game that isn't simply a point and click or shoot-em-up.  It is an exercise of the mind.  Enjoy!
